name: PCWH syndrome (SOX10)
aliases: Waardenburg syndrome type 4 with neurological involvement

clinicalPearls: A severe neurocristopathy caused by variants in SOX10, a transcription factor essential for neural crest and glial development; the acronym denotes Peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, Central dysmyelination, Waardenburg syndrome and Hirschsprung disease
It sits at the severe end of the SOX10-related Waardenburg-Shah (type 4) spectrum, uniting features that would otherwise be considered separate disorders
Waardenburg features include sensorineural hearing loss and pigmentary anomalies such as a white forelock, heterochromia iridis and patchy skin or hair depigmentation
Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic megacolon) causes neonatal intestinal obstruction and chronic constipation and reflects failure of enteric neural crest migration

The neurological picture combines a central hypomyelinating or dysmyelinating leukodystrophy with a peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, producing motor delay, spasticity, ataxia and neuropathic weakness
Diagnosis is clinical pattern recognition of this striking combination, supported by MRI showing central dysmyelination and by nerve conduction studies, and confirmed by SOX10 testing
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, including surgical treatment of Hirschsprung disease, hearing rehabilitation, and physiotherapy and developmental support
reference.pathophysiology: PCWH is caused by heterozygous variants in SOX10, a transcription factor that governs the development, migration and differentiation of neural crest cells and their derivatives, including melanocytes, enteric ganglia, and both Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes. Disruption of SOX10 function impairs multiple neural crest lineages simultaneously: defective melanocyte and inner-ear development produces the Waardenburg pigmentary and auditory features, failed enteric ganglion formation causes Hirschsprung disease, and impaired Schwann cell and oligodendrocyte function produces combined peripheral demyelinating neuropathy and central dysmyelination. Certain variants that escape nonsense-mediated decay are thought to exert dominant-negative effects, contributing to the severe combined phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Waardenburg syndrome types 1 to 4 without the full neurological involvement
Isolated Hirschsprung disease (RET and other genes)
Charcot-Marie-Tooth and other hereditary demyelinating neuropathies
Other neurocristopathies with pigmentary and enteric features
Congenital sensorineural hearing loss of other genetic causes
additionalInvestigations: SOX10 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis to confirm the diagnosis
Brain MRI to demonstrate central dysmyelination or hypomyelination
Nerve conduction studies to characterise the peripheral demyelinating neuropathy
Audiological assessment for sensorineural hearing loss
Contrast enema and rectal biopsy where Hirschsprung disease is suspected
Ophthalmology and dermatology review for pigmentary features
redFlags: Neonatal intestinal obstruction or enterocolitis from Hirschsprung disease requiring urgent surgical management
Respiratory compromise from combined central and peripheral neuromuscular involvement
Progressive weakness or loss of motor milestones
reference.prognosis: PCWH is a severe, multisystem disorder and prognosis depends on the combined burden of neurological, enteric and sensory involvement; the central and peripheral myelin disease contributes to significant motor and developmental disability. Early surgical management of Hirschsprung disease and coordinated supportive care influence outcome, but the overall course is serious.
pitfalls: Treating the Waardenburg, Hirschsprung and neurological features as unrelated rather than recognising a single SOX10 disorder
Overlooking the peripheral neuropathy when central dysmyelination is evident, or vice versa
Missing Hirschsprung disease as a cause of neonatal obstruction or refractory constipation
Attributing hearing loss and pigmentary changes to isolated Waardenburg syndrome without pursuing the broader phenotype
Failing to provide genetic counselling, including for de novo dominant variants
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Manage Hirschsprung disease surgically with resection of the aganglionic segment and a pull-through procedure, and treat neonatal obstruction and enterocolitis
Rehabilitate the sensorineural hearing loss with hearing aids or cochlear implantation and early auditory-verbal support
Treat the spasticity of the combined central dysmyelination and peripheral neuropathy with physiotherapy, antispasticity agents such as baclofen, and orthoses
Support motor development and neuropathic weakness through coordinated physiotherapy, occupational therapy and mobility aids
Provide nutritional support and manage bowel dysfunction and feeding difficulties
Offer ophthalmology and dermatology review for the pigmentary anomalies and monitor for related complications
Arrange genetic counselling, noting most SOX10 variants arise de novo, and coordinate care through a multidisciplinary neurogenetic team
